channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: Feeling the strain of the party frenzy
item.description: Keith Dunstan surveys the exhausting social demands of the Christmas party season, from the strain of remembering names after the divorce revolution to a handy list of conversation-starter topics for the desperate guest.

item.title: Melbourne's massage industry
item.description: Social welfare researcher Bronwen Rumbold lifts the lid on Melbourne's reputation as the massage parlour capital of the world, tracing the city's 300-plus parlours, their links to migration patterns and organised crime, and the Social Welfare Department's cautious attempts at reform.

item.title: Not just an ordinary, run-of-the-mill academic
item.description: A tribute to Monash University historian Ian Turner, who died on Erith Island on 27 December 1978 — former communist, carriage cleaner, jazz lover, Richmond football fanatic, and one of the most gifted lecturers Australia produced.

item.title: The era of musical cohabitants
item.description: The cohabitation revolution has swept through Dunstan's social circle — from the Baptist mother making quilts for her daughter's new arrangement to Californian "palimony" cases — and he proposes the newspapers add Cohabitations and Dehabitations to their classified columns.

item.title: Passionate paintings by an old commo
item.description: Noel Counihan, at 65, holds a retrospective exhibition at Realities Gallery in Toorak — the converted church hall where some of us went to kindergarten — and talks about four decades of social-conscience painting, his communist years, street-meeting arrests, and why showing your work is like being naked in a room.

item.title: Let's get back to service with a snarl
item.description: Dunstan rails against the American import of compulsory cheerfulness — from "Have a nice day" butchers to name-tagged bank tellers — and laments the passing of the honest Australian grunt.

item.title: Melbourne gets behind Moomba
item.description: On its 25th anniversary, Dunstan traces the turbulent history of Moomba — from its disputed Aboriginal name meaning "let's get together and have fun" to the dramas of sinking gondolas, a cable tram wreck, Rolf Harris and the garbage strike, and Mickey Mouse's pie in the face.

item.title: The garish grandeur of the bottom end
item.description: The "Chicago end" of Collins Street — the block of William Pitt's exuberant Land Boom buildings including the Rialto — faces a development battle, and Planning Minister Alan Hunt has declared a three-month freeze while a British expert recommends recycling the entire block.

item.title: Art lovers in transports of delight
item.description: Melbourne has fallen in love with its trams and commissioned six leading artists — including Mirka Mora, Clifton Pugh and Andrew Southall — to paint them as moving canvases; Dunstan explores the resulting "tramurals" and their unlikely origin stories.

item.title: All out for National Strike Day
item.description: With Melbourne deep in its annual strike season — railways, power workers, teachers and bank employees all walking out — Dunstan proposes a National Strike Festival in mid-March and outlines his business plan for the Melbourne Strike Emporium, to be headquartered at the Regent Theatre.

item.title: As torpid as Gomorrah on a rainy Sunday
item.description: Germaine Greer attacks Melbourne as dull and boring, but Keith Dunstan mourns that the city's magnificent old torpor is being steadily destroyed by Sunday trading, hotel bars, one-day cricket, Collins Street towers, and a Truth newspaper full of explicit sex advertisements that would have shocked Gomorrah itself.

item.title: Governors are on a good wicket
item.description: Keith Dunstan surveys Australian governors since World War II and finds the job goes overwhelmingly to generals and lawyers, suggesting it is time for imagination — and nominating ABC cricket commentator Alan McGilvray as the ideal candidate.

item.title: It's always been 'last in is lousy'
item.description: Professor Geoffrey Blainey warns that Asian immigration is "well ahead of public opinion," prompting Keith Dunstan to survey Australia's long history of racism — from the Chinese, Irish, Italians and Turks to the treatment of Aborigines — and observe that it has always been the latest arrivals who cop it.

item.title: Like filling the MCG with objets d'art
item.description: Melbourne's Arts Centre, fifteen years in the making and finally opening in May 1984, gets Keith Dunstan's grand tour — from the underground theatres floating in primeval swamp mud, to Sidney Nolan's gift of 1350 Paradise Gardens paintings written on a plain sheet of paper, to the 75,000 floating brass baubles in the State Theatre ceiling.

item.title: The battle of the MCG
item.description: The Melbourne Cricket Club faces a deadly battle as the VFL demands Grand Final rights at the MCG, forcing MCC members from their stand, while the government drives reforms on women's membership and threatens legislation — leaving members wondering what equity they have in their own ground.

item.title: Getting our government on the ball
item.description: Australia is turning into a sportocracy — VFL champion Kevin Bartlett is crowned King of Moomba, footballers seek parliamentary pre-selection, Robert de Castella wins Australian of the Year, and Bob Hawke rides his sporting connections to a record 73 percent approval rating. Keith Dunstan proposes a fully sporting cabinet led by Alan Bond.

item.title: The need for kneecappery
item.description: This has been a vintage summer for knees — Peter McNamara's reconstructed cruciate ligament, Graham Yallop's medial ligament, Garry Sidebottom's knee — leading Keith Dunstan to propose an Australian Foundation of Kneecappery and chairs of Cartilology at our universities.

item.title: How I learned to love my computer
item.description: After two months of living with a Tandy TRS80 personal computer, Keith Dunstan reports on his turbulent apprenticeship — the joy of silent 5am keystrokes, the terror of losing whole stories to the electronic void, the global-search miracle, and a 75,000-word spelling dictionary that is making Batman copy pure for the first time in 25 years.

item.title: Pari Tab could save us all
item.description: Frank Hardy laments Australia's guilt-ridden TAB with no lavatories or cafe comforts, while Victoria prepares to introduce Pub TAB and Footy TAB — inspiring Keith Dunstan to propose Parl TAB (bet on ministerial resignations and royal commissions), Crick TAB, and Train TAB to get John Cain's Government out of the red.

item.title: The bagnio capital of the world
item.description: Victoria's Minister for Planning announces the decriminalisation of prostitution in massage parlours, prompting Keith Dunstan to survey Melbourne's long history with the "social evil" — from 597 fallen women in 1885, to the Duke of Edinburgh's visit to Sarah Fraser's bagnio in Stephen Street in 1867, to the 190 parlours now serving 60,000 to 70,000 clients a week.

item.title: Cinders – it's back to the ball
item.description: Keith Dunstan travels by K-class steam locomotive to celebrate the centenary of T94 at the North Williamstown Railway Museum — 21 steam locomotives, a magnificent 1890 Norman car used by Victorian governors and royalty, and a coming Steam Age Australia luxury excursion service modelled on the Orient Express.

item.title: Let's move Sunday to Saturday
item.description: Melbourne's cherished sepulchral Sunday is being eroded by incremental liberalisations — Sunday hotel trading, soccer at the MCG — while hardware merchant Frank Penhalluriack wages a ten-year battle from South Caulfield, paying over $130,000 in fines. Keith Dunstan's new campaign: shift everything to Sunday and have absolutely nothing on Saturday.

item.title: Australia's longest-running election
item.description: The Melbourne Anglican diocese has spent nearly a year trying to elect a new archbishop to replace the departed Archbishop Dann, with two board members themselves candidates, constant leaks splitting the board, and an open letter suggesting Alan Bond — his dedication to causes well known, his media image well managed — as a suitable alternative.

item.title: Pools: a gum tree's favorite friend
item.description: Domestic Bliss No 2 — Keith Dunstan's swimming pool, lifted over the house by a crane when first installed, has proved a fountain of misery and expense: pump repairs, chlorine bills, leaves from the liquidambar and the lemon-scented gum, and a pool turned swamp-green while the owners were overseas. A friend in Moorabbin has shown the way — he gave his fibre-glass pool away on a truck and planted roses instead.

item.title: Ned is now among the real money
item.description: At Glenrowan, insurance broker Bob Hempel has spent $500,000 — vastly more than Ned ever stole — creating a Disneyland-style Kelly show with computerised smoke, articulated robots, real rain down a window, a pub going up in flames on hidden gas jets, and Ned himself at the trap door with drums rolling. Business has been beautiful.

item.title: A life of domestic bliss
item.description: Keith Dunstan surveys the security-obsessed miseries of modern Melbourne domestic life — deadlocked out of his own house in dirty jeans, keys locked inside a thief-proof car at the seaside, an RACV man defeated after 45 minutes, and a locksmith who charges $70 to work his way in after dark.

item.title: A festival of light beers
item.description: Courage and Carlton have both launched low-alcohol beers in Melbourne — Dunstan taste-tests both and concludes the random breath-test regime is driving a genuine market revolution, though an anomaly in NSW law keeps them out of Sydney.

item.title: How the footy is going to the dogs
item.description: Weekly VFL attendances have drifted from 9 percent of Melbourne's population in 1930 to 4.45 percent in 1984, five clubs are technically bankrupt, and North Melbourne ruckman Gary Dempsey warns the game is dying. Premier Cain has offered to help enforce player contracts, the VFL president wants a national competition of 16 teams, and international soccer has arrived — Paolo Rossi's dinner seat at the St Kilda Town Hall cost $5000.

item.title: The art of spending pennies
item.description: The Rialto, William Pitt's magnificent 1891 Victorian Gothic building at the western end of Collins Street, is being recycled into the grand Menzies at the Rialto hotel — but its refurbishment stalls when the Historic Buildings Council insists on preserving the corrugated iron lavatory cubicles at the end of its galleries, arguing they tell the not-so-glorious story of "Smelbourne" in the 1880s, when night-soil men collected waste and the urinals drained into the Yarra.

item.title: I just lap up this computer
item.description: Following the April instalment on his Tandy TRS80 desktop, Keith Dunstan has acquired a Tandy TRS80 Model 100 lap computer — small enough for a briefcase, operable on a plane or on the dunny — and rapturously reports its built-in software, Big Ben chimes, Find function for phone numbers and the astonishing ability to zap copy over any telephone in the world.
